title: Concept Drills — Chemistry of Non-Metals (Class 11 Chemistry)
subject: chemistry

questions.question: Why do non-metals tend to act as oxidising agents while metals act as reducing agents?
questions.solution: Non-metals have high electron affinity and nearly full valence shells — they GAIN electrons (oxidising others, reducing themselves). Metals have low ionisation energies — they LOSE electrons easily (reducing others). Position on the periodic table sets the electron-transfer direction.

questions.question: Diamond and graphite are both pure carbon yet behave oppositely (hard insulator vs soft conductor). Explain with structure.
questions.solution: Diamond: each C bonds to 4 others in a 3D tetrahedral network (sp³) — rigid, no free electrons, hardest natural solid. Graphite: each C bonds to 3 in flat hexagonal layers (sp²) with delocalised electrons — layers slide (lubricant) and the π electrons conduct. Same element, different bonding geometry, opposite properties.

questions.question: How does the acid–base character of oxides change across period 3 (Na₂O → MgO → Al₂O₃ → SiO₂ → P₄O₁₀ → SO₃ → Cl₂O₇)? Explain the trend.
questions.solution: Strongly basic (Na₂O) → weakly basic (MgO) → amphoteric (Al₂O₃) → weakly acidic (SiO₂) → strongly acidic (P₄O₁₀, SO₃, Cl₂O₇). Cause: across the period the element's electronegativity rises, so the E–O bond becomes more COVALENT and the oxide more acidic; down a group, oxides become more basic (more ionic). Metallic → non-metallic character is mirrored in oxide behaviour.

questions.question: Why does fluorine displace chlorine, bromine and iodine from their salts, but not the reverse?
questions.solution: Reactivity follows oxidising power: F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂ (smallest atom, highest electron affinity/electronegativity). A stronger oxidant displaces a weaker one from its halide — F₂ takes electrons from Cl⁻, but Cl₂ cannot oxidise F⁻. The displacement series is the oxidising-power ranking in action.

questions.question: Why does lead(II) compounds form more readily than lead(IV), unlike carbon which is tetravalent?
questions.solution: Down group 14, the ns² pair becomes increasingly reluctant to participate in bonding (poor shielding by d and f electrons, relativistic stabilisation) — the INERT PAIR effect. So the +2 state (using only p electrons) grows more stable down the group; carbon's 2s² is NOT inert, giving C its +4 chemistry.

questions.concept: Why nitrogen is unreactive despite abundance
questions.question: Air is 78% N₂ yet nitrogen is chemically sluggish. What structural feature causes this?
questions.solution: The N≡N triple bond (bond energy ~941 kJ/mol) plus the absence of a low-energy dipole or lone-pair reactivity makes the molecule very hard to break. All nitrogen chemistry in industry must first defeat that triple bond — which is why ammonia synthesis needs high pressure, temperature and a catalyst. Abundance of an element says nothing about the reactivity of its common form.

questions.question: Graphite conducts and diamond does not, though both are pure carbon. Why?
questions.solution: Allotropes differ in the arrangement of atoms. Diamond has a rigid tetrahedral sp³ network with all four valence electrons locked in sigma bonds — no mobile carriers. Graphite is layered sp² with one delocalised p-electron per carbon, forming a conducting sheet. Same element, different bonding topology, radically different properties. Structure, not composition, sets behaviour.

questions.question: Why do SO₂ and NOₓ from combustion end up as acid rain, while CO₂ (also non-metal oxide) mainly does not?
questions.solution: SO₂ and NOₓ oxidise in the atmosphere with water and oxygen to H₂SO₄ and HNO₃ — strong acids that fully dissociate and lower the rain's pH substantially. CO₂ forms carbonic acid, a weak acid that only partly dissociates, so it acidifies only mildly. The difference is the acid STRENGTH of the resulting oxyacid, not the fact of being a non-metal oxide.
